keyVerseText: I also will do this unto you; I will even appoint over you terror, consumption, and the burning ague, that shall consume the eyes, and cause sorrow of heart: and ye shall sow your seed in vain, for your enemies shall eat it. over: Heb. upon
rootMeaning: The Hebrew verb דּוּב (dûwb) is a primitive root that fundamentally conveys the idea of sorrow expressed through physical and emotional decline, specifically to pine away or waste away. Unlike the simple English word 'sorrow,' this root captures a vivid picture of gradual weakening or fading, often linked to the soul's distress. This deep sense of pining away enriches the understanding of sorrow as not merely an emotional state but a consuming process that affects one's vitality and life force.
usageInScripture: This word appears only once in Scripture, specifically in Leviticus 26:16, where it is translated as 'cause sorrow.' The limited occurrence highlights its specialized use to describe a profound effect of divine judgment that leads to inner anguish and physical wasting. The consistent translation focusing on sorrow and consumption reveals its role in illustrating the severe consequences of disobedience, emphasizing both emotional and corporeal suffering.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding דּוּב (dûwb) as a verb that means to cause one to pine away deepens our grasp of the biblical portrayal of sin's consequences and God's discipline. It highlights how spiritual rebellion leads not only to external punishment but to an internal decay of the soul, reflecting the seriousness with which God views covenant unfaithfulness. This word reminds believers that sorrow and suffering are not merely incidental but can be instruments used by God to bring about repentance and restoration. Christ’s redemptive work ultimately addresses this pining away by offering renewal and healing to the weary soul, fulfilling the hope beyond mere sorrow.
keyVerseReflection: Leviticus 26:16 states, 'I also will do this unto you; I will even appoint over you terror, consumption, and the burning ague, that shall consume the eyes, and cause sorrow of heart.' Here, דּוּב (dûwb) enriches the depiction of divine judgment by emphasizing that the punishment will not only afflict the body but will deeply afflict the heart with sorrow. This sorrow is not superficial grief but a profound pining that affects the very life of the people, underscoring the gravity of turning away from God's covenant.
